title: Opportunity is a readiness ecology, not an exam result: educators connect young people’s pathways to skills, place, support, and confidence
source_unit: UK Department for Work and Pensions / YouGov, Survey of Education Professionals: Young People and Work Report, August 27, 2026
geography: Great Britain; teachers and education professionals surveyed through the YouGov panel

observations.period: March 2026 survey fieldwork, published August 27, 2026; perceived drivers of opportunity

denominator.unit: teachers and education professionals in Great Britain

motivation.unit: percent identifying motivation as affecting young people’s access to employment, education, or training

work_readiness.unit: percent identifying work-readiness skills such as organization, time management, and teamwork

local_opportunities.unit: percent identifying availability of local jobs or opportunities

confidence.unit: percent identifying confidence as affecting access

readiness_ecology.value: Educators describe opportunity as a compound system of personal readiness, social support, local labor demand, and confidence rather than a qualification-only outcome.

observations.method: Online YouGov survey of education professionals on behalf of DWP; fieldwork in March 2026; the report presents weighted reporting-sample estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The respondents report professional perceptions rather than young people’s observed outcomes; the survey is not a causal evaluation of motivation, work-readiness, or local opportunity.
observations.subgroup: Teachers and education professionals in Great Britain.
observations.counterinterpretation: Professionals may use broad readiness language to describe institutional difficulty, and motivation may partly reflect prior opportunity, health, family support, or labor-market conditions.

observations.period: March 2026 survey fieldwork, published August 27, 2026; curriculum legitimacy

denominator.unit: teachers and education professionals in Great Britain

too_much_exam_focus.unit: percent saying there is too much focus on passing exams

not_enough_work_preparation.unit: percent saying there is not enough focus on preparing young people for work and employment

not_enough_soft_skills.unit: percent saying there is not enough focus on soft skills for work and employment

broaden_without_lowering_standards.unit: percent agreeing the curriculum could include more work-related knowledge and skills without lowering academic standards

curriculum_conversion.value: The legitimacy problem is framed as balance, not a choice between academic standards and employability: educators want multiple forms of readiness recognized by the system.

observations.method: Cross-sectional survey of education professionals with forced-choice and agreement items on curriculum priorities.
observations.uncertainty: These are professional judgments about curriculum emphasis, not measures of actual teaching time, student attainment, or employer outcomes.
observations.subgroup: Teachers and education professionals in Great Britain.
observations.counterinterpretation: Perceived exam overemphasis may reflect wider frustration with transitions into work rather than a direct curriculum effect.

observations.period: March 2026 survey fieldwork, published August 27, 2026; route diversification

denominator.unit: teachers and education professionals in Great Britain

careers_guidance_support.unit: percent supporting careers guidance through schools, sixth forms, and colleges

applied_vocational_support.unit: percent supporting greater access to applied or vocational pathways before age 16

alternative_pathways_support.unit: percent supporting alternative pathways for young people who struggle with the current curriculum

route_diversification.value: Strong support for multiple routes suggests that education legitimacy is increasingly tied to whether different strengths and learning needs can reach credible work and further-learning pathways.

observations.method: Cross-sectional survey with support estimates for careers, applied/vocational, and alternative pathways.
observations.uncertainty: Support for a pathway does not establish funding, availability, quality, completion, employer recognition, or equitable access.
observations.subgroup: Teachers and education professionals in Great Britain.
observations.counterinterpretation: High support may reflect general approval of guidance and choice rather than agreement on implementation, sequencing, or resource allocation.

observations.period: March 2026 survey fieldwork, published August 27, 2026; engagement and work-experience barriers

denominator.unit: teachers and education professionals in Great Britain

low_motivation_barrier.unit: percent identifying low motivation or interest as a barrier to engagement before age 16

parental_influence_barrier.unit: percent identifying parental influence as a barrier

send_support_barrier.unit: percent identifying lack of SEND support as a barrier

mental_health_barrier.unit: percent identifying mental-health challenges as a barrier

work_experience_effectiveness.unit: percent of secondary teachers considering their school effective at providing good-quality work experience; 29% said not effective

engagement_conversion.value: Readiness is also an institutional-access problem: support, family context, health, peers, and the quality of work experience shape whether a pathway can be used.

observations.method: Cross-sectional survey of education professionals, including subgroup reporting for secondary teachers and schools with different free-school-meal eligibility levels.
observations.uncertainty: Barrier estimates reflect professional attribution and may bundle school, family, health, and labor-market mechanisms; work-experience effectiveness is not observed placement quality or student outcome.
observations.subgroup: Teachers and education professionals; secondary teachers for work-experience estimates.
observations.counterinterpretation: Professionals may attribute engagement barriers to students or families when institutional design, transport, discrimination, or resource constraints also contribute.

related_sources.claim: Official DWP publication containing the YouGov sample, fieldwork, education-professional findings, subgroup boundaries, and implementation limits.
The companion general-population polling provides a separate public-attitude route and is not merged with professional perceptions in this record.

boundary: This record adds an education-to-work opportunity route: professionals describe employability as a readiness ecology shaped by work-readiness, confidence, local opportunity, transport, health, SEND support, family context, and work experience, alongside academic attainment. It does not establish young people’s actual transitions, causal curriculum effects, pathway quality, or employer outcomes. The source is a DWP-commissioned YouGov online panel of professional perceptions.

reproduction_audit.retrieval_hash_scope: The official GOV.UK DWP report was reviewed for publication date, sample, fieldwork, methodology, opportunity drivers, curriculum judgments, pathway support, engagement barriers, work-experience estimates, and source boundaries.
